options: Shows nginx's logged entries and continues to follow new ones live, as they're written
Only shows logs from before the current boot
Permanently deletes all of nginx's log history
Restarts the nginx service immediately
questions.explain: -u filters to the nginx unit and -f follows the log live, the journalctl equivalent of tail -f.

questions.q: Which log file specifically records authentication activity like SSH logins and sudo commands?
options: /etc/passwd
/var/log/syslog only
journalctl -b
/var/log/auth.log (or /var/log/secure on RHEL-based systems)
questions.explain: auth.log (Debian/Ubuntu) or secure (RHEL-based) is dedicated to authentication events, separate from the general system log.

questions.q: What is tail -f used for, and how does it differ from grep?
options: tail -f and grep are interchangeable and do the exact same thing
tail -f deletes a log file; grep creates one
grep only works on journalctl output, never on plain log files
tail -f watches a log live as new lines are written; grep filters existing lines down to ones matching a pattern
questions.explain: tail -f is for watching a log live; grep is for searching/filtering text already in a file — they're often combined, not interchangeable.

questions.q: According to this lesson's troubleshooting workflow, what should you check first when a service seems down?
options: The entire /var/log/syslog file from the beginning
systemctl status <service>, to confirm whether it's even running
Rebooting the whole server immediately
journalctl -b, regardless of which service is affected
questions.explain: The workflow goes from specific to broad: service status first, then that service's own logs, then the wider system log.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend checking a specific service's status and logs before the wider system log?
options: It's required by systemd and will error otherwise
The system-wide log never contains useful information
Most problems — a crash on startup, a config typo, a port conflict — show up clearly at the specific level, so starting broad wastes time
systemctl and journalctl don't work unless syslog is checked first
questions.explain: Starting specific (status, then that service's logs) catches most issues directly; the broad system log is mainly needed when the service itself looks healthy.
